title: Multi-Die Assemblies Dominate At 2nm And Below
gist: Multi-die assemblies and heterogeneous integration are becoming the default at 2nm and below because a single reticle-sized die can no longer deliver the performance AI workloads demand, shifting the industry's value and bottlenecks toward interposers, advanced packaging, thermal management, and the enormous compute needed to design and mask these systems. Executives from Lam Research, ASE, Amkor, Intel, IBM, Arm, Silvaco, and Synopsys describe interposers scaling to 40X reticle, two-phase cooling, three-track standard cells, virtual fabs, and mask compute costs approaching 1 million CPU hours per layer.

insights.claim: The core driver of multi-die adoption is that a single reticle-sized die can no longer hold enough transistors to meet AI workload performance demands, creating a performance gap that feature shrinks cannot close.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Value migrates from pure lithographic shrink toward packaging, interposers, and interconnect — favoring OSATs and packaging-tool suppliers relative to node-only plays.
insights.quote: demand for faster processing has far outpaced the ability to scale transistors and wires, creating a performance gap that feature shrinks can’t close
insights.locator: The primary driver behind this long-anticipated shift

insights.claim: Agentic AI breaks the homogeneous-GPU data center model: it requires CPUs alongside GPUs and accelerators to orchestrate agents across highly customized, shifting workloads, pushing designs toward heterogeneous multi-die assemblies.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Watch for accelerator mix shift in AI capex — a rising CPU/accelerator content per rack undercuts the pure-GPU-count framing of AI demand.
insights.quote: Agentic AI requires CPUs, in addition to GPUs and various accelerators, to orchestrate how agents behave in highly customized, shifting workloads.
insights.locator: The rapid adoption of agentic AI only complicates matters

insights.claim: The design space for heterogeneous systems has grown so large that AI is now required just to validate chip architectures and confirm a design is manufacturable, testable, and still relevant by the time it ships into a larger system.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Structural tailwind for EDA vendors selling AI-driven architectural exploration and manufacturability sign-off, not just point tools.
insights.quote: AI is needed even to validate chip architectures and ensure what gets designed is manufacturable, testable, and still relevant by the time it’s integrated into a larger heterogeneous system
insights.locator: The result is so many variables and options

insights.claim: Many engineering teams are targeting at least two orders of magnitude improvement in performance per watt, a goal the article argues requires a complete realignment of the chip industry rather than incremental node progress.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: A 100x perf/watt bar means no single vendor or technology captures it — expect spending spread across packaging, memory, and architecture simultaneously.
insights.quote: Many engineering teams aim for at least two orders of magnitude improvement in performance per watt.
insights.locator: Many engineering teams aim for at least two orders

insights.claim: Reaching 100x performance-per-watt at the edge will likely depend on in-memory, near-memory, and in-sensor pre-processing to cut the data volume processed, plus smaller language models and quantization and pruning of all language models.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Edge AI silicon economics favor memory-centric and sensor-side compute suppliers over raw TOPS vendors; model compression becomes a hardware requirement, not an optimization.
insights.locator: In addition, and especially as AI moves to the edge

insights.claim: When foundries and packaging houses now cite reticle limits, they mean interposer size multiples, not the fixed 858mm2 maximum EUV lithography exposure.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: A vocabulary trap for investors reading roadmap claims — 'reticle size' announcements are packaging capability, not lithography progress.
insights.quote: when foundries and packaging houses talk about reticle limits these days, they typically are referring to the much larger interposer size, not the maximum lithography exposure, which is fixed at 858mm2 for EUV
insights.locator: Today, many chiplets are at, or close to, full reticle size

insights.claim: ASE says the industry is currently at 5.5X reticle interposers with 9X, 12X, and 40X on the roadmap ahead.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: A concrete roadmap milestone to track for packaging capex — each step up in interposer multiple raises panel/wafer handling and yield requirements.
insights.quote: Now we are on 5.5X, and 9X, 12X, and 40X are ahead.
insights.locator: The reticle size is really increasing a lot

insights.claim: 2.5D adoption is heavily weighted toward large data centers because a bespoke multi-die assembly deployed across tens of thousands of servers achieves its own economies of scale, but that economic logic does not transfer outside that application.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Advanced-packaging demand stays concentrated in hyperscale until cost innovations land — a narrow customer base and a concentration risk for packaging suppliers.
insights.quote: A bespoke multi-die assembly that can be deployed in tens of thousands of servers achieves its own economies of scale, but it doesn’t work outside of that particular application.
insights.locator: This explains why 2.5D adoption is heavily weighted

insights.claim: Organic interposer research began across the industry in 2010 and glass interposer research at Georgia Tech in 2011, yet both took roughly 15 years to reach mainstream discussion — a concrete measure of the semiconductor industry's risk aversion and adoption lag.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Calibrates timelines: novel packaging materials announced today are ~10-15 years from volume, so near-term revenue theses on them are usually early.
insights.quote: The chip industry is extremely risk-averse because the cost of failure in the fab — or worse, in the field — is enormous.
insights.locator: Interposer alternatives gain traction

insights.claim: Glass interposers trade brittleness and difficult via drilling for fewer parasitics than silicon and extreme flatness, which matters increasingly in large advanced packages.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Flatness advantage scales with interposer size — glass gets structurally more attractive as the industry moves toward 9X-40X reticle packages.
insights.quote: But glass has fewer parasitics than silicon, and it’s extremely flat, which is important in advanced packages.
insights.locator: The main problem with glass is its brittleness

insights.claim: High-density fan-out with bridges is emerging as a way to displace stacks of expensive RDL layers, with ASE describing replacing high-density multi-layer RDL with a bridge while only one to three RDL layers handle the less-dense routing.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: A cheaper path to interposer-class density — watch bridge adoption as the cost-down lever that could broaden advanced packaging beyond hyperscalers.
insights.quote: there is a lot of discussion about replacing those high-density, multiple RDL layers with a bridge, so the rest of the less-dense fan-out is taken care of by only one or three layers of RDL
insights.locator: You can have three, six, or nine layers

insights.claim: Data center logic utilization is pushing into the 70% to 80% range versus 5% to 15% at the turn of the Millennium, when cooling only required a fan — a roughly 5-10x rise in sustained thermal load per unit of silicon.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: The single cleanest quantification of why liquid cooling capex is non-optional; sizes the addressable shift for cooling vendors.
insights.quote: As a point of reference, server utilization at the turn of the Millennium was in the 5% to 15% range, when cooling only required a fan.
insights.locator: One of the thorniest issues in packaging is thermal dissipation

insights.claim: No single cooling approach is sufficient anymore, so chipmakers must combine options from a menu including rack liquid cooling, in-chip microchannels, direct cooling, cold plates, immersion, vapor caps, and TSV chimneys — and when that still falls short, fall back to throttling schemes like checkerboarding, where every other transistor or block of transistors is turned on and off.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Cooling is a stacked bill of materials rather than a winner-take-all bake-off, and thermal throttling means deliverable compute per package can sit below its nameplate.
insights.quote: some type of throttling, like checkerboarding, can be used, where every other transistor or block of transistors is turned on and off
insights.locator: Today, no single approach is sufficient

insights.claim: Amkor identifies two-phase cooling — a non-conductive low-boiling-point liquid circulated across a cold plate in a closed loop — as the next big transition, because boiling holds a constant temperature and the resulting turbulence sharply cuts interface resistance.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: A named next-generation cooling transition from an OSAT executive — track two-phase design wins as the leading indicator of the next module power step-up.
insights.quote: Two-phase cooling is coming, and that significantly reduces the interface resistance of getting the heat out
insights.locator: A new approach combines several of these options

insights.claim: Package power has risen enough that test programs must now be co-designed with the customer to power up different parts of the chip at different times, or the heat overwhelms the tester's ability to run the part.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: A hidden cost and cycle-time driver in the back end — thermal-constrained test raises test time per unit and favors ATE vendors with thermal control.
insights.quote: They’re turning on different parts of the chip at different times so we don’t overwhelm the ability to test from a heat standpoint.
insights.locator: Getting the heat out is a huge challenge

insights.claim: Intel's assembly and test R&D leadership names mechanical warpage and thermal dissipation as the two biggest issues in advanced packaging, ahead of the interconnect and density problems that get more attention, while arguing improved multi-physics modeling now catches hot spots at floor-planning time and feeds layout changes back to silicon designers.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Mechanical reliability, not electrical performance, is the likely source of the next packaging yield surprise — and some thermal spend can be avoided in EDA rather than in hardware.
insights.quote: Mechanical warpage and thermal dissipation will be the biggest issues.
insights.locator: The thermal team is looking at various ways

themes.theme: IBM nanostack and the 3T cell race

insights.claim: IBM Research has developed a hybrid stacking approach that angles transistors using beveled edges and fewer metal routing tracks, claiming 50% improved performance, 70% more energy efficiency, and 40% more SRAM, with production expected in the early 2030s.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: A dated, quantified roadmap claim to hold vendors to — early-2030s production means it affects node economics after 2nm/A14, not current capex cycles.
insights.quote: The result is increased transistor density — 50% improved performance, 70% more energy efficiency, and 40% more SRAM.
insights.locator: New stacking approach

insights.claim: IBM claims a first three-track (3T) standard cell library, enabled by using different substrates for the nFET and pFET plus a standard-cell layout innovation, versus five-track as today's industry best with four-track as the intermediate step.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Cell height, not gate pitch, is becoming the density lever — a metric to watch in foundry roadmap claims alongside nanometer labels.
insights.quote: Five-track today is the industry’s best, then it moves to four-track, and then three-track.
insights.locator: We believe that with the introduction of different substrates

insights.claim: IBM's beveled nanostack preserves the ability to route signals and power on both sides of the wafer, an advantage over aligned CFETs where everything but the top and bottom transistor faces must route laterally and waste layout area.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: A concrete architectural argument that the CFET consensus path has a layout-efficiency flaw — relevant to who wins the post-2nm transistor race.
insights.quote: If the transistors are aligned like CFETs, you cannot do that. You can only access the top of the top transistor and the bottom of the bottom transistor. Everything else has to go laterally, which takes up area in your layout.
insights.locator: Then there’s a third innovation

insights.claim: IBM says it has at least three generations of nanostack available without stacking additional layers, and that stacks can go to at least four layers if liquid microchannel cooling, thermal vias, and possibly a new higher-thermal-conductivity substrate are added.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Three node-equivalent generations without added stacking layers is a cheap runway claim — but it makes cooling a prerequisite for transistor scaling itself.
insights.quote: We have at least three generations of nanostack without stacking more layers.
insights.locator: We can put signal routing and power routing

insights.claim: IBM argues design technology co-optimization is no longer sufficient and that mechanical and thermal factors must be built into the technology from the start, because mechanical stability cannot be addressed after the fact.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Expands the EDA tool requirement set into mechanical and thermal simulation — an adjacency opportunity for multi-physics simulation vendors.
insights.quote: Mechanical cannot be addressed after the fact. It has to be part of the technology.
insights.locator: Previously, the most advanced designs were done

themes.theme: The chiplet marketplace that never arrived

insights.claim: Despite chiplets shipping in production since 2011 and DARPA's 2017 CHIPS program funding standardized components, nearly all chiplet-based designs remain custom and no successful commercial chiplet marketplace has emerged beyond standard I/Os and high-bandwidth memory.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Deflates the merchant-chiplet-ecosystem investment thesis after nearly a decade of funding — chiplet exposure is really exposure to a handful of large systems companies.
insights.quote: Beyond standard I/Os and high-bandwidth memory, a successful commercial chiplet marketplace has yet to emerge.
insights.locator: Chiplets

insights.claim: Arm reports that chiplet interoperability standards are fragmenting in practice because Nvidia, Arm, and Google each push different approaches, and that on close examination chiplets become more expensive than expected with unclear reusability.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: A candid vendor admission that the standards story is broken — treat chiplet-standard adoption headlines skeptically until one approach consolidates share.
insights.quote: But Nvidia pushes one thing, we push another, Google pushes another. So where do we meet? When you talk to customers and really start digging into it, it becomes more expensive than you thought.
insights.locator: We’ve looked at chiplets, and at first it seems

insights.claim: The technical reason chiplets resist commoditization is that each chiplet must be fully characterized in the context of what physically surrounds it — noise, heat, vibration, voltage changes — plus the workloads it will run, all of which affect its utilization, size, and system performance per watt.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Context-dependence is a structural, not temporary, barrier to a plug-and-play chiplet market — reduces the probability of a merchant chiplet business ever scaling.
insights.quote: But integrating chiplets into an advanced package is far more complicated than snapping LEGOs together.
insights.locator: The underlying problem is that when chiplets are encapsulated

insights.claim: Even the large systems companies that justified custom chiplet costs appear to be facing cost pressure, evidenced by recent moves to sell chiplets designed for internal use — Google's TPUs, Meta's inference accelerators, Amazon's CPUs and AI training and inference chips, and Microsoft's training and inference accelerator.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Hyperscalers externalizing in-house silicon signals cost pressure, not strength — and creates a new merchant-accelerator competitive set against Nvidia and AMD whose success is unproven.
insights.quote: It’s still unclear how these in-house designs will fare against designs from other companies.
insights.locator: But even they appear to be facing cost pressures

insights.claim: Large automakers including BMW, Stellantis, Volkswagen, Rivian, and Tesla are developing chiplet-type architectures intended to serve different options across all of their car models, while also debating whether generic hardware with a virtualization layer or common programming interface could substitute.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Automotive is the second potential volume market for chiplets after hyperscale — but the generic-hardware alternative is a live threat to that demand pool.
insights.locator: Large automotive companies, such as BMW

insights.claim: Imagination Technologies frames chiplet viability as a data-movement question — bandwidth, latency, and hop count — noting that if data stays local a chiplet behaves like a normal SoC, but three or four hops to main memory at hundreds of cycles each becomes much more problematic.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: A usable screen for evaluating any chiplet architecture claim: count the hops to main memory before believing the performance numbers.
insights.quote: If it’s all local data, fantastic. That’s like a normal SoC. But if we need to do three or four hops to get to main memory, and it takes hundreds of cycles for each hop, it’s much more problematic.
insights.locator: There’s a lot of work when we’re building chiplets

insights.claim: The unlock for multi-die design is that available compute finally lets chipmakers brute-force complex design and manufacturing problems and integrate previously siloed steps end-to-end, replacing a highly iterative, rigidly siloed, time-consuming process.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: AI compute is both the demand driver and the enabling tool for the next chip generation — a reflexive loop that supports sustained EDA and compute spend.
insights.quote: What’s changed is the massive compute power that has since become available, allowing chipmakers to use that same compute power to brute-force complex design and manufacturing challenges, then integrate all the steps end-to-end.
insights.locator: Big changes with massive simulations

insights.claim: Lam Research says simulation has crossed from an academic pursuit taking nine months to prove a mechanism into hour-by-hour, day-to-day predictive use — work that would have been intractable even 10 to 15 years ago on memory, compute, and algorithmic grounds.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: R&D cycle time is compressing at equipment vendors — a margin and time-to-market lever that is hard to see in reported financials until it shows up in node cadence.
insights.quote: Simulation used to be an academic pursuit. Somebody used to take nine months to run simulations to prove a mechanism or effect. Today, we’re doing in an hour what was completely unimaginable 20 years ago
insights.locator: We have a much-improved understanding

insights.claim: Silvaco reports enormous demand for surrogate machine learning models and digital twins of individual fab processes, driven by process complexity and prototype wafer cycle times now measured in months.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Virtual process development is a revenue line to watch at TCAD vendors — its growth is driven by wafer cycle-time cost, which rises with node complexity.
insights.quote: We’re seeing enormous demand for building surrogate or machine learning models, digital twins, whatever you want to call them, for particular processes
insights.locator: We’ve got this long history of multi-physics solvers

insights.claim: The binding constraint on fab ML models is data sharing, not algorithms: synthetic data must be calibrated against physical data, but no one in the semiconductor industry allows anyone else to see their physical data.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Proprietary fab data is the real moat in AI-for-semiconductor-manufacturing — favors incumbents with installed tool fleets over pure software startups.
insights.quote: And the problem with the physical data is nobody in the semiconductor industry allows anyone else to see their physical data.
insights.locator: The challenge, and one that has persisted for decades

themes.theme: 2nm mask compute becomes a cost center

insights.claim: SRAM's failure to scale, with no other memory type working as well, forces explicit prioritization of what lives in SRAM versus off-chip DRAM and blunts the performance benefit of shrinking features — though scaling still reduces power at each node, which matters most for compute-intensive AI.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Node shrinks are now bought for power, not speed — reframes what a foundry node transition is actually worth to a customer.
insights.quote: The problem is that SRAM doesn’t scale, and no other memory type works as well, so what gets stored in SRAM versus off-chip DRAM needs to be prioritized.
insights.locator: Continued scaling

insights.claim: Multi-die assemblies typically mix processing elements built at different nodes, with only the highest-priority computations placed on the most advanced nodes.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Leading-edge wafer demand per system is lower than headline chip counts imply — mature-node capacity retains structural demand inside AI systems.
insights.quote: multi-die assemblies typically have a variety of processing elements developed at different nodes, with the most advanced nodes running the highest-priority computations
insights.locator: In fact, multi-die assemblies typically have a variety

insights.claim: At 2nm and below the failure modes compound: process variation, faster circuit aging, greater susceptibility to noise and voltage swings, and much harder-to-control gate leakage, which Synopsys characterizes as amplified versions of 3nm and 4nm challenges.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Reliability and aging tooling become mandatory spend at 2nm — a growth vector for silicon lifecycle management and in-chip monitoring vendors.
insights.quote: The challenges are basically more severe versions of the 3nm and 4nm nodes, which are amplified at 2nm and below
insights.locator: At 2nm and below, problems compound

insights.claim: Synopsys quantifies mask computation cost at roughly 1 million CPU hours per mask for a full reticle-size chip on a hard layer, meaning 10 to 20 hard layers implies about 20 million CPU hours per product.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Computational lithography is now a hard-dollar per-product cost — quantifiable compute demand that scales with every new tapeout at advanced nodes.
insights.quote: To compute a full reticle-size chip, it takes roughly 1 million CPU hours for one mask. For a relatively hard layer, like a middle-metal layer mask, you need 1 million CPU hours.
insights.locator: In my group, day in and day out

insights.claim: A foundry processing 10 products per month faces roughly 200 million CPU hours per month, or 6.5 million CPU hours per day, requiring about 300,000 cores — roughly 120 racks at 15 kilowatts per rack — just for mask computation.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Foundries are becoming large-scale compute buyers themselves; a ~1.8MW captive cluster per 10 products/month is a new, under-modeled line of semiconductor capex.
insights.quote: That means you need roughly 300,000 cores in your data centers, which translates to about 120 racks in a data center at 15 kilowatts per rack.
insights.locator: So if you are a foundry and you have to process 10 products

insights.claim: The same DUV and EUV hardware used at 7nm, 5nm, and 4nm is being carried into 2nm and below, shifting the burden onto heavy computation and mask optimization to widen the process window, which translates directly into yield.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Advanced-node yield is increasingly a software and compute problem rather than a tool-purchase problem — reweights value toward computational lithography software.
insights.quote: A lot of the weight is shifting to doing more heavy computation and optimization to compute the optimal mask, so that if you stick it into the scanner, it will give you the best process window.
insights.locator: Another thing at play is the level of hitting the dimensions

insights.claim: In the short term, fab and packaging capacity — not technology availability — will determine which companies get access to advanced-node technology, a constraint the article expects to even out over the next five years.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Allocation, not capability, is the near-term competitive moat — favors incumbents with locked-in foundry and OSAT capacity through roughly 2031.
insights.quote: the availability of some of these may be determined by fab and packaging capacity, which will limit the number of companies with access to advanced-node technology, but that will even out over the next five years
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: The longer-term question is not whether leading-edge technology will be available everywhere but how and where it gets used, which will vary greatly by region, market segment, and workload — with power priorities differing sharply between an AI data center in China and one in the United States.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Expect regionally divergent silicon requirements rather than a single global spec — a fragmentation risk for vendors betting on one optimized product line.
insights.quote: the focus on power will vary greatly from an AI data center in China to one in the United States
insights.locator: Longer term, the big question isn’t whether

insights.claim: Progress in multi-die assemblies now depends on industry-wide methodology development rather than single-company breakthroughs, a shift institutionalized when the ITRS ended in 2015 because planar scaling stopped delivering PPA benefits and was replaced in 2016 by IEEE's IRDS covering packaging, materials, quantum computing, yield, and lithography.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: The IRDS roadmap is the coordination mechanism to watch for which packaging and materials paths get industry-wide investment and therefore scale economics.
insights.quote: That effort ended in 2015 because it became clear that planar device scaling no longer provided sufficient power, performance, and area benefits.
insights.locator: In the past, much of this was achieved through the consensus
